newsitem.title: USA: U.S. URGED TO END QUARTERLY SUGAR IMPORT LIMITS.
newsitem.headline: U.S. URGED TO END QUARTERLY SUGAR IMPORT LIMITS.

text.p: The Dominican Republic and other sugar exporters have urged the United States to loosen restrictions on shipments under an annual U.S. import quota.

In comments filed with the U.S. Agriculture Department (USDA), the exporters generally praised a new system that the United States implemented last year for administering the quota. But they urged changes that they said would make it more manageable for exporters.
The U.S. divides its import quota among about 40 countries based on their share of the U.S. market in 1976-82, the last time U.S. sugar imports were not governed by a quota.
The Dominican Republic has the the largest share of the import quota, followed by the Philippines and Brazil. Together, the three countries control 44 percent of U.S. sugar imports.
For the current quota year, which ends September 30, USDA eliminated quarterly restrictions on shipments from Australia, the fourth-largest quota holder.
But for the Big Three, it restricted quarterly shipments to 25 percent of their annual quota allocation. Unused portions were allowed to be shipped in subsequent quarters.
Separate comments filed by a Brazilian sugar trade group and the Brazilian embassy in Washington also requested an end to quarterly shipping restrictions.
Other exporter comments focused on the size of a "stocks-to-use ratio" trigger used to determine the overall quota and the timing of subsequent quota allocations during the course of the year.
USDA initially set the fiscal 1997 sugar import quota at 2.3 million tonnes, but only allocated 1.7 million tonnes at the start of the year.

The remaining 600,000 tonnes were scheduled to allocated in tranches of 200,000 each in January, March and May -- assuming that the projected sugar stocks-to-use ratio in each of those months remained below 15.5 percent.
That ratio compares annual consumption to projected ending stocks to guage whether supplies are plentiful.
In January, the fiscal 1997 stocks-to-use ratio rose above 15.5 percent and USDA canceled 200,000 tonnes of the quota. However, the March and May tranches went ahead as scheduled.

In its comments, the Brazillian Association of Sugar and Alcohol Producers of the State of Alagoas in Brazil urged the trigger be set between 16 to 17 percent to allow more sugar to enter the United States.

The trade group also urged that 90 percent-- instead of 70 percent-- of the initial quota be allocated at the start of the year and that subsequent allocations be made in December, February and April, instead of January, March and May.
The Mauritius Sugar Syndicate also urged that subsequent allocations come earlier in the quota year to give small exporters more time to arrange shipments.
